purpose: Explicit source selections for the four newly authorized Pāli chapters; pāda positions refer to this importer's shad-delimited native chapter stream, not Sanskrit stanza numbers.

selections.note: The Tibetan witness contrasts a hundred meaningless stanzas with one meaningful word, whereas Pāli has a thousand words. Its native numerical wording is retained.

No sufficiently close distinct Tibetan counterpart was established for Pāli101 in the consulted concordance and native comparison. The shared wording of the neighboring hundred-stanzas comparison is not duplicated here to create a second apparent witness.

Related passage only: the Tibetan witness contrasts monthly thousandfold offerings over a century with faith in the Buddha. Pāli contrasts them with momentary homage to a developed person. The shared sacrifice comparison does not establish an exact verse counterpart; this provisional partial is excluded from secure Tibetan coverage.
The native Tibetan verse has six pādas. Its homage to a person cultivating the self is retained, with no wording added from Pāli.

No sufficiently close Tibetan Udānavarga counterpart to the four blessings from honoring elders was established in the consulted concordance and native comparison. This is not a claim of absence elsewhere in Tibetan literature.
The native Tibetan shorter-life expression is a few days (ཉིན་ཞག་འགའ་ཞིག), rather than the Pāli one day; it is retained.

The Tibetan witness concerns the unchanging state (གོ་འཕང་མི་གཡོ); Pāli names the deathless state. These are related recensional expressions, not identical words. The native Tibetan shorter-life expression is a few days (ཉིན་ཞག་འགའ་ཞིག), rather than the Pāli one day; it is retained.

Rockhill’s concordance identifies Tibetan24.10, concerning the state difficult to see, with Pāli115, which concerns the supreme Dhamma. The common century-versus-short-life comparison is retained, but this is a partial correspondence in content. The different Tibetan predicate has not been replaced by a closer-sounding stanza from elsewhere in its expanded series. The native Tibetan shorter-life expression is a few days (ཉིན་ཞག་འགའ་ཞིག), rather than the Pāli one day; it is retained.
This native passage is Tibetan5.16 in Rockhill; Sanskrit Uv5.15 is a different edition’s reference. Tibetan preserves the three watches of the night.
The Tibetan counterpart is a four-pāda stanza whose first and third pādas repeat establishing oneself properly. Its longer native pādas have not been divided or rewritten to imitate Pāli.

The Derge witness ends by finding joy through taming oneself. Rockhill renders the corresponding ending as the difficulty of self-restraint; the Derge wording is retained and is not harmonized with either his translation or Pāli.
The Tibetan counterpart is the patron-in-oneself stanza (Rockhill23.20) from an expanded self-as-refuge series. The Sanskrit reference Uv23.11 is not assigned to the Tibetan text.
Tibetan preserves six pādas about rejecting the teaching under a bad view and a bamboo destroyed by its own fruit. Its native stanza length is retained.
Tibetan has six pādas, including purity and impurity being one’s own doing. The shorter preceding two-pāda karma maxim has not been substituted for this passage.

The full Tibetan bodily-restraint, non-harming, deathless-state counterpart is in chapter7 (Rockhill7.7), independently checked in Derge. Rockhill’s index instead points to the related chapter20.19; that printed cross-reference is not imposed on this native selection.

This directly checked Tibetan counterpart is Rockhill15.8: wakeful effort, day-and-night study, devotion to the deathless, and exhaustion of taints. It is omitted from his final Pāli index, illustrating why that index alone is a lower bound.

The Tibetan29.51 stanza corresponds to the Pāli229–230 pair. Its first four pādas are aligned here; the final two, including the gold comparison, are aligned at230. This division is editorial and preserves native word order.

Only the last two pādas of Tibetan29.51 are aligned here: none should blame such people, like Jambu-island gold ornaments. The Pāli clauses about gods and Brahmā are not present in this selection. This is labelled a partial counterpart, not padded out with a modern translation.
The Tibetan counterpart adds reaching the deathless state and going without sorrow to the restraint of body, speech, and mind. All six native pādas are retained.
The Tibetan stanza has six pādas, adding a statement about distance from the taintless state. It is a historical counterpart with additional material.
Tibetan has eight pādas here, including bodily mindfulness and an added closing taintless-state statement. Native length and order are retained.
The mother/father/two-kings/kingdom stanza is in Tibetan chapter33.70, not Sanskrit chapter29.24. Its Tibetan wording and source location independently establish the counterpart.
The Tibetan mother/father/two-kings/tiger stanza is in chapter33.71. The closing description and the two kings’ wording are retained as this recension gives them.
Tibetan15.18 is the bodily-mindfulness member of the expanded awakening series; Sanskrit15.15 is a cross-reference in another edition, not this source’s number.
The non-harming member is Tibetan15.21, within a larger series that also names non-ill-will, concentration, emptiness, and other practices.
The meditation member is Tibetan15.22; Sanskrit15.25 is not used as a Tibetan number.
The native Tibetan counterpart contrasts difficult renunciation and household life and repeated suffering. It is in the Śramaṇa chapter, outside the Tibetan Miscellaneous chapter.
The Tibetan witness emphasizes generosity and the abandonment of stinginess alongside faith and virtue. It has not been rewritten to reproduce the Pāli list of reputation and wealth.
The Tibetan counterpart stands in the Self chapter as Rockhill23.2. It retains single sitting/bedding, absence of sloth, dwelling alone in the forest, and taming oneself.
